subject: Medicine
topic: Acute Ischemic Stroke and Blood Pressure Permissive Thresholds for Thrombolysis
stem:
A 64-year-old man is brought to the emergency department by ambulance 75 minutes after the sudden onset of right-sided facial droop, right arm weakness, and severe expressive aphasia. He has a history of essential hypertension and type 2 diabetes mellitus. On physical examination, he is alert but unable to speak fluently, following one-step commands with difficulty. Neurological examination reveals dense right hemiplegia (motor strength 0/5 in right upper extremity, 2/5 in right lower extremity), right facial flattening, and expressive aphasia, yielding a National Institutes of Health Stroke Scale (NIHSS) score of 16. Emergent non-contrast head computed tomography (CT) reveals no acute intracranial hemorrhage, mass effect, or early ischemic changes (Alberta Stroke Program Early CT Score [ASPECTS] is 10). Blood glucose is 142 mg/dL, and platelet count is 260,000/mm3. Vital signs demonstrate blood pressure of 198/112 mm Hg, heart rate of 88/min, and respiratory rate of 16/min. The patient has no history of head trauma, prior stroke, gastrointestinal bleeding, or anticoagulant use.

Which of the following represents the most appropriate immediate management step before administering intravenous thrombolytic therapy?

options.text: Administer intravenous labetalol (10 to 20 mg over 1 to 2 minutes) or nicardipine infusion to reduce blood pressure below 185/110 mm Hg prior to initiating intravenous alteplase or tenecteplase
options.explanation: For patients with acute ischemic stroke presenting within the 4.5-hour thrombolytic window, intravenous thrombolysis (alteplase 0.9 mg/kg or tenecteplase 0.25 mg/kg) improves functional neurological outcomes. However, ELEVATED BLOOD PRESSURE IS A CRITICAL CONTRAINDICATION TO THROMBOLYSIS: (1) Safety Threshold: Intravenous thrombolysis cannot be administered if systolic blood pressure exceeds 185 mm Hg or diastolic blood pressure exceeds 110 mm Hg, because arterial hypertension markedly increases the risk of catastrophic symptomatic intracranial hemorrhage (sICH). (2) Management: Guidelines (AHA/ASA) mandate immediate active blood pressure lowering to SBP < 185 mm Hg and DBP < 110 mm Hg prior to thrombolysis, typically using intravenous labetalol (10-20 mg IV push, may repeat once) or a titratable nicardipine infusion (5-15 mg/h). (3) Post-Thrombolysis Target: Once thrombolysis is initiated, blood pressure must be rigorously maintained below 180/105 mm Hg for at least the subsequent 24 hours. If blood pressure cannot be maintained below 185/110 mm Hg, intravenous thrombolytic therapy must not be administered.

options.text: Immediately infuse intravenous alteplase 0.9 mg/kg while permitting blood pressure to remain at 198/112 mm Hg to preserve collateral penumbral cerebral perfusion
options.explanation: Administering intravenous thrombolytic therapy with blood pressure > 185/110 mm Hg causes a dramatic surge in fatal symptomatic intracranial hemorrhage; lowering BP below 185/110 is an absolute prerequisite.

options.text: Administer intravenous nitroprusside bolus targeting an immediate reduction of systolic blood pressure to 120 mm Hg
options.explanation: Precipitous blood pressure reduction below 140 mm Hg in acute ischemic stroke collapses cerebral perfusion pressure across the ischemic penumbra, precipitating irreversible infarct expansion.

options.text: Administer oral aspirin 325 mg and clopidogrel 300 mg immediately, withholding thrombolysis due to the elevated blood pressure
options.explanation: Hypertension is readily treatable with IV labetalol or nicardipine; withholding thrombolytic therapy in an eligible patient presenting at 75 minutes with severe deficits (NIHSS 16) causes permanent severe disability.

options.text: Perform emergent lumbar puncture to rule out subarachnoid hemorrhage before administering antihypertensive therapy
options.explanation: Non-contrast head CT has > 95% sensitivity for subarachnoid hemorrhage within the first 6 hours; lumbar puncture is unnecessary, delays thrombolysis, and introduces an arterial puncture site contraindicating thrombolysis.

subject: Medicine
topic: Large Vessel Occlusion (LVO) and Endovascular Thrombectomy
stem:
A 72-year-old woman is brought to the hospital by her daughter. The patient was last known to be at her normal neurological baseline when going to bed at 10:00 PM the previous evening. At 7:00 AM this morning (9 hours after last known well), her daughter found her slumped in a chair, mute, with flaccid paralysis of the left face, arm, and leg. On examination, the patient has forced right gaze deviation, left homonymous hemianopsia, profound left hemiplegia, and complete hemineglect, corresponding to an NIHSS score of 20. Non-contrast head CT reveals no hemorrhage and an ASPECTS score of 8. CT angiography (CTA) of the head and neck demonstrates an acute, complete occlusion of the M1 segment of the right middle cerebral artery. CT perfusion (CTP) imaging reveals an ischemic core volume (cerebral blood flow < 30%) of 18 mL and a total hypoperfused penumbra volume (Tmax > 6 seconds) of 110 mL, yielding an absolute mismatch volume of 92 mL and a mismatch ratio of 6.1. Vital signs show blood pressure of 158/88 mm Hg, heart rate of 76/min, and oxygen saturation of 97% on ambient air.

Which of the following represents the most appropriate next step in the management of this patient?

options.text: Administer intravenous tenecteplase 0.25 mg/kg bolus, withholding mechanical intervention
options.explanation: Intravenous thrombolysis is restricted to within 4.5 hours of last known well in routine clinical practice; this patient is 9 hours from last known well and thrombolysis is contraindicated.

options.text: Perform emergent mechanical endovascular thrombectomy with a stent retriever or contact aspiration catheter
options.explanation: Mechanical Endovascular Thrombectomy (EVT) has transformed the management of acute ischemic stroke secondary to Large Vessel Occlusion (LVO) of the anterior circulation (internal carotid artery or M1 segment of the middle cerebral artery). (1) TRADITIONAL WINDOW: EVT is standard of care within 6 hours of symptom onset. (2) EXTENDED WINDOW (6 TO 24 HOURS): Landmark trials (DAWN and DEFUSE-3) established that EVT provides profound clinical benefit in patients presenting between 6 and 24 hours from last known well (including wake-up strokes) when physiological imaging demonstrates a SALVAGEABLE PENUMBRA: (a) Small ischemic core (infarcted tissue that cannot be saved, typically core volume < 50-70 mL on CT perfusion or diffusion-weighted MRI), and (b) Large mismatch ratio (penumbra to core ratio >= 1.8, mismatch volume >= 15 mL) or clinical-core mismatch (high NIHSS >= 10 with small core). (3) APPLICATION: This patient presents at 9 hours with an M1 occlusion, a tiny core of only 18 mL, and a massive mismatch volume of 92 mL (ratio 6.1), representing substantial salvageable brain tissue at risk. Immediate mechanical thrombectomy is indicated. (Note: Intravenous alteplase is only FDA-approved up to 4.5 hours from last known well and is not indicated here at 9 hours).

options.text: Initiate oral aspirin 325 mg and high-intensity atorvastatin 80 mg daily, admitting to the neuro step-down unit for conservative therapy
options.explanation: Conservative antiplatelet therapy for acute anterior circulation LVO with large salvageable penumbra results in massive complete middle cerebral artery infarction, brain herniation, and death or severe dependency in > 80% of patients.

options.text: Administer continuous intravenous unfractionated heparin infusion targeting an activated partial thromboplastin time (aPTT) of 60 to 80 seconds
options.explanation: Therapeutic heparin in acute ischemic stroke does not improve clinical outcomes and significantly increases intracranial hemorrhagic transformation.

options.text: Perform emergent right hemicraniectomy prior to any vascular revascularization attempts
options.explanation: Decompressive hemicraniectomy is a surgical rescue for life-threatening malignant cerebral edema with midline shift, not an initial treatment for acute revascularizable large vessel occlusion.

subject: Medicine
topic: Status Epilepticus Pharmacotherapy Escalation Sequence
stem:
A 34-year-old woman with a history of focal epilepsy is brought to the emergency department by paramedics in active generalized tonic-clonic status epilepticus. Paramedics administered intravenous lorazepam 4 mg en route 10 minutes ago, but continuous convulsive motor activity persisted. Upon arrival in the resuscitation bay, she remains actively seizing with continuous generalized clonic movements of all four extremities, rhythmic eye blinking, and jaw clenching. Vital signs demonstrate blood pressure of 148/92 mm Hg, heart rate of 132/min, respiratory rate of 22/min, and oxygen saturation of 94% on a non-rebreather mask. Fingerstick blood glucose is 118 mg/dL. A second dose of intravenous lorazepam 4 mg is administered immediately. Five minutes later (total seizure duration now 25 minutes), continuous bilateral clonic motor activity persists without cessation.

Which of the following represents the most appropriate next pharmacological intervention?

options.text: Administer a third and fourth dose of intravenous lorazepam 4 mg every 5 minutes until convulsive movements cease
options.explanation: Repeated benzodiazepine dosing beyond 2 adequate doses fails because synaptic GABA-A receptors become internalized; it risks respiratory arrest while delaying definitive second-line therapy.

options.text: Initiate oral carbamazepine suspension via a nasogastric tube at a dose of 200 mg every 8 hours
options.explanation: Carbamazepine is an oral agent with slow absorption and erratic bioavailability; it has no role in the urgent management of status epilepticus.

options.text: Administer intravenous levetiracetam (60 mg/kg, maximum 4,500 mg) or intravenous fosphenytoin (20 mg PE/kg) as a second-line urgent antiseizure medication
options.explanation: Status epilepticus (SE) is defined as continuous seizure activity lasting >= 5 minutes, or two or more seizures without full recovery of consciousness between them. As seizure activity continues beyond 10 to 30 minutes, GABA-A receptors undergo rapid clathrin-mediated internal endocytosis from synaptic membranes, leading to pharmacodynamic TOLERANCE to benzodiazepines, while excitatory NMDA receptors proliferate. PHARMACOTHERAPY ESCALATION (AES GUIDELINES / ESETT TRIAL): (1) PHASE 1 (0 to 10 min): Initial emergent therapy is a parenteral benzodiazepine: intravenous lorazepam (0.1 mg/kg, typically 4 mg IV push, repeated once at 5-10 min) or intramuscular midazolam (10 mg IM). (2) PHASE 2 (10 to 30 min - URGENT CONTROL): If seizure activity persists after two full doses of benzodiazepines, repeating further benzodiazepines causes respiratory arrest and hypotension without seizure cessation due to GABA receptor downregulation. The mandatory next step is administration of a NON-BENZODIAZEPINE SECOND-LINE ANTISEIZURE MEDICATION given as a rapid intravenous infusion. The landmark ESETT (Established Status Epilepticus Trial) trial demonstrated that LEVETIRACETAM (60 mg/kg IV, max 4,500 mg), FOSPHENYTOIN (20 mg PE/kg IV, max 1,500 mg PE), and VALPROATE SODIUM (40 mg/kg IV, max 3,000 mg) have equivalent efficacy (~45-50% seizure termination at 60 min) and safety profiles. (3) PHASE 3 (> 30-40 min - REFRACTORY SE): If seizures continue despite second-line therapy, the patient has refractory status epilepticus requiring endotracheal intubation and continuous anesthetic infusions (propofol, midazolam, or ketamine).

options.text: Administer continuous intravenous neuromuscular blockade with vecuronium to abolish skeletal muscle contractions
options.explanation: Paralytics abolish peripheral muscle contractions but leave cortical electrical status epilepticus entirely unsuppressed, causing ongoing excitotoxic cerebral necrosis while masking seizures.

options.text: Administer intravenous mannitol 1 g/kg to reduce presumptive acute cerebral edema
options.explanation: Osmotic therapy with mannitol is indicated for intracranial hypertension and herniation, not for terminating cortical epileptic seizure discharges.

subject: Medicine
topic: Spontaneous Intracerebral Hemorrhage (ICH) and Anticoagulation Reversal
stem:
A 76-year-old man with non-valvular atrial fibrillation managed with oral apixaban (5 mg twice daily; last dose taken 4 hours ago) presents to the emergency department with sudden severe headache, vomiting, and acute left-sided weakness that began 90 minutes ago. Physical examination reveals an obtunded man with Glasgow Coma Scale score of 10 (E2V3M5). Neurological examination demonstrates dense left hemiplegia and left facial droop. Vital signs show blood pressure of 192/108 mm Hg, heart rate of 82/min, and respiratory rate of 18/min. Non-contrast head CT demonstrates an acute 32-mL hyperdense intraparenchymal hematoma within the right basal ganglia (putamen) with 4 mm of midline shift and surrounding vasogenic edema, with no intraventricular extension. Laboratory evaluation reveals platelet count of 210,000/mm3, serum creatinine of 1.1 mg/dL, and prothrombin time/INR of 1.4.

Which of the following represents the most appropriate immediate medical management strategy for this patient?

options.text: Immediate administration of intravenous idarucizumab followed by blood pressure reduction targeting systolic blood pressure < 110 mm Hg
options.explanation: Idarucizumab is a monoclonal antibody fragment specific for dabigatran (direct thrombin inhibitor); it has zero activity against apixaban (factor Xa inhibitor). Furthermore, lowering SBP < 110 mm Hg causes acute kidney injury and hypoperfusion.

options.text: Transfusion of 4 units of fresh frozen plasma and 2 units of platelets, while maintaining systolic blood pressure at 160 to 180 mm Hg to preserve cerebral perfusion
options.explanation: FFP takes hours to thaw and infuse, causes severe volume overload, and fails to rapidly reverse factor Xa inhibitors; platelets are harmful in non-thrombocytopenic ICH (PATCH trial).

options.text: Immediate administration of high-dose intravenous dexamethasone 10 mg to reduce perihematomal vasogenic edema
options.explanation: Systemic corticosteroids in acute spontaneous ICH have no benefit, significantly increase infectious and hyperglycemic complications, and increase mortality.

options.text: Immediate intravenous administration of andexanet alfa (or 4-factor prothrombin complex concentrate if unavailable) combined with rapid intravenous blood pressure lowering targeting a systolic blood pressure between 130 and 140 mm Hg
options.explanation: Spontaneous Intracerebral Hemorrhage (ICH) in the setting of oral anticoagulant therapy is an extreme medical emergency carrying a 30-day mortality approaching 50%, primarily driven by early hematoma expansion within the first 6 to 24 hours. Emergency management requires two simultaneous, time-critical interventions: (1) IMMEDIATE ANTICOAGULATION REVERSAL: For direct oral factor Xa inhibitors (apixaban, rivaroxaban) ingested recently, the specific reversal agent is intravenous ANDEXANET ALFA (a recombinant modified human factor Xa decoy protein that binds and sequesters factor Xa inhibitors with high affinity). If andexanet alfa is unavailable or contraindicated, 4-factor Prothrombin Complex Concentrate (4F-PCC; 50 U/kg IV) should be immediately administered. Fresh frozen plasma (FFP) is inadequate due to volume overload and slow reversal. (2) ACUTE BLOOD PRESSURE CONTROL: Elevated systolic blood pressure drives persistent extravasation and hematoma expansion. Landmark randomized clinical trials (INTERACT-2, ATACH-2) and the AHA/ASA 2022 Guidelines recommend rapid, smooth blood pressure reduction using titratable intravenous agents (e.g., nicardipine or labetalol) to a TARGET SYSTOLIC BLOOD PRESSURE OF 130 TO 140 MM HG. ATACH-2 demonstrated that targeting SBP < 130 mm Hg precipitously (e.g., < 120 mm Hg) increased renal adverse events without clinical benefit; thus, 130-140 mm Hg is the optimal safe target range.

options.text: Administration of intravenous protamine sulfate and vitamin K 10 mg slow IV push
options.explanation: Protamine reverses unfractionated heparin, and vitamin K reverses warfarin (takes 12-24 hours); neither has any activity against apixaban.

subject: Medicine
topic: Aneurysmal Subarachnoid Hemorrhage (aSAH) and Vasospasm Prevention
stem:
A 48-year-old woman is brought to the emergency department after experiencing a sudden, explosive headache ('the worst headache of my life') while lifting weights at the gym 3 hours ago, followed by several episodes of vomiting and transient loss of consciousness. On arrival, she is alert and oriented but in severe pain with marked photophobia and neck stiffness (positive Kernig and Brudzinski signs). Neurological examination reveals no focal cranial nerve or motor deficits (Hunt and Hess Grade 2; World Federation of Neurosurgical Societies Grade 1). Emergent non-contrast head CT demonstrates extensive hyperattenuating blood filling the basal cisterns, sylvian fissures, and fourth ventricle (Fisher Grade 3). CT angiography of the cerebral circulation reveals a 6-mm saccular aneurysm of the anterior communicating artery with an irregular dome. Vital signs demonstrate blood pressure of 144/86 mm Hg, heart rate of 78/min, and core body temperature of 37.1 C.

In addition to urgent neurointerventional consultation for aneurysm securing, which of the following represents the most appropriate pharmacotherapy to improve neurological outcomes and prevent delayed cerebral ischemia?

options.text: Administer continuous intravenous nimodipine infusion at 2 mg/hour to achieve rapid and reliable plasma concentrations
options.explanation: Intravenous administration of nimodipine is strictly contraindicated by the FDA (black box warning) because it causes catastrophic, refractory systemic cardiovascular collapse and death.

options.text: Initiate aggressive prophylactic 'Triple-H therapy' with aggressive hypervolemic fluid loading (5 liters/day normal saline) to achieve a CVP > 12 mm Hg
options.explanation: Prophylactic hypervolemia and hemodilution are obsolete; they cause pulmonary edema, congestive heart failure, and hyponatremia without preventing vasospasm. Guidelines recommend euvolemia.

options.text: Administer intravenous magnesium sulfate continuous infusion targeting a supra-therapeutic serum magnesium of 4.5 to 5.5 mg/dL
options.explanation: The MASH-2 trial demonstrated that routine magnesium infusions do not reduce delayed cerebral ischemia or improve neurological outcomes in aneurysmal SAH.

options.text: Administer high-dose intravenous methylprednisolone 500 mg every 12 hours to suppress meningeal inflammatory irritation
options.explanation: Systemic corticosteroids do not improve clinical outcomes in aneurysmal subarachnoid hemorrhage and increase risks of hyperglycemia and infection.

options.text: Initiate oral or nasogastric nimodipine (60 mg every 4 hours for 21 consecutive days) while maintaining strict euvolemia with isotonic crystalloids
options.explanation: Aneurysmal Subarachnoid Hemorrhage (aSAH) carries significant morbidity and mortality from two distinct phases: (1) EARLY REBLEEDING: Maximal in the first 24 hours (~4-10%); prevented by prompt surgical clipping or endovascular coiling. (2) DELAYED CEREBRAL ISCHEMIA (DCI) / VASOSPASM: Typically occurs between days 4 and 14 post-hemorrhage (peaking at days 7-10), caused by toxic breakdown products of subarachnoid erythrocyte lysis (oxyhemoglobin, endothelin-1, free radicals) inducing microvascular spasm, cortical spreading depolarization, and cerebral infarction. PHARMACOTHERAPY AND PREVENTION (AHA/ASA GUIDELINES): (a) NIMODIPINE: Oral or enteral nimodipine (60 mg every 4 hours for 21 days) is the ONLY medication proven in randomized clinical trials to reduce poor neurological outcomes and cerebral infarction in aSAH. It acts as a lipophilic dihydropyridine calcium channel blocker with cerebrovascular selectivity and neuroprotective cytoprotective effects. It MUST BE ADMINISTERED ORALLY OR VIA NASOGASTRIC TUBE; INTRAVENOUS NIMODIPINE IS STRICTLY PROHIBITED due to severe fatal systemic hypotension. (b) VOLEMIC STATUS: Strict EUVOLEMIA must be maintained using isotonic intravenous fluids (0.9% normal saline). Routine 'Triple-H therapy' (hypervolemia, hemodilution, hypertension) is OBSOLETE; prophylactic hypervolemia causes pulmonary edema and myocardial ischemia without improving outcomes.

subject: Medicine
topic: Myasthenic Crisis Management and Airway Triage
stem:
A 46-year-old woman with generalized myasthenia gravis managed with oral pyridostigmine (60 mg four times daily) and prednisone (10 mg daily) is brought to the emergency department with severe, rapidly progressive generalized weakness, difficulty swallowing saliva, and shortness of breath over the past 24 hours. She was prescribed oral ciprofloxacin for an uncomplicated urinary tract infection 2 days ago. Physical examination demonstrates an anxious woman sitting upright with weak, muffled speech and tachypnea. She is unable to count past 12 on a single breath. Bilateral ptosis and moderate facial weakness are present. Vital signs reveal blood pressure of 142/88 mm Hg, heart rate of 118/min, respiratory rate of 28/min, and oxygen saturation of 94% on room air. Bedside pulmonary function testing demonstrates:
- Forced vital capacity (FVC): 14 mL/kg (normal > 60 mL/kg; baseline 38 mL/kg 3 months ago)

topic: Guillain-Barré Syndrome (GBS) Respiratory Monitoring and Therapy
stem:
A 28-year-old man presents to the hospital with a 4-day history of progressive ascending weakness and tingling that began in his feet and has now ascended to involve both thighs and hands. He had an episode of self-limited watery diarrhea 3 weeks ago while traveling in Mexico. On physical examination, he has symmetric flaccid weakness of both lower extremities (motor strength 2/5 proximally, 1/5 distally) and upper extremities (4/5 proximally, 3/5 distally). Deep tendon reflexes are completely absent (0/4) throughout all four limbs. Sensation to light touch and vibration is mildly diminished in a stocking-glove distribution. Cranial nerves are intact, but he reports mild difficulty clearing throat secretions. Vital signs show blood pressure of 138/82 mm Hg, heart rate of 96/min, respiratory rate of 22/min, and oxygen saturation of 97% on ambient air. Bedside spirometry demonstrates a forced vital capacity (FVC) of 22 mL/kg (normal > 60 mL/kg) and negative inspiratory force (NIF) of -26 cm H2O.

Which of the following represents the most appropriate initial management strategy for this patient?

options.text: Administer high-dose intravenous methylprednisolone 1,000 mg daily for 5 days to halt inflammatory autoimmune nerve demyelination
options.explanation: Systemic corticosteroids are ineffective and contraindicated in Guillain-Barré syndrome; multiple clinical trials demonstrated that steroids do not accelerate recovery and may slow axonal repair.

options.text: Admit to an intensive care unit for serial bedside pulmonary function tests (FVC and NIF every 4 to 6 hours) and initiate intravenous immunoglobulin (IVIG) or plasma exchange, avoiding systemic corticosteroids
options.explanation: Guillain-Barré Syndrome (GBS, acute inflammatory demyelinating polyradiculoneuropathy [AIDP]) is an autoimmune polyradiculoneuropathy frequently triggered by molecular mimicry following Campylobacter jejuni enteritis. (1) RESPIRATORY MONITORING: The most critical determinant of immediate survival is monitoring for impending diaphragmatic and intercostal muscle paralysis. Up to 30% of patients require mechanical ventilation. Pulse oximetry and arterial blood gases are dangerously insensitive because hypoxemia and hypercapnia develop only after diaphragmatic collapse occurs. Patients must be admitted to an ICU with serial monitoring of Forced Vital Capacity (FVC) and Negative Inspiratory Force (NIF) every 4 to 6 hours. The '20/30/40 rule' mandates elective mechanical ventilation when: (a) FVC drops < 15 to 20 mL/kg, (b) NIF becomes less negative than -30 cm H2O, or (c) Maximum expiratory pressure drops < 40 cm H2O. (2) DISEASE-MODIFYING IMMUNOTHERAPY: Intravenous Immunoglobulin (IVIG, 0.4 g/kg/day for 5 days) or Plasma Exchange (PLEX, 5 sessions over 2 weeks) accelerates motor recovery and reduces time on mechanical ventilation. Both have equivalent efficacy; combination therapy provides no additional benefit. (3) CONTRAINDICATION TO CORTICOSTEROIDS: Multiple large randomized controlled trials (including Cochrane systematic reviews) prove that SYSTEMIC CORTICOSTEROIDS (oral or intravenous) PROVIDE ZERO BENEFIT IN GBS AND MAY ACTUALLY DELAY OR PROTRACT MOTOR RECOVERY.

options.text: Administer combination therapy with simultaneous intravenous immunoglobulin and therapeutic plasma exchange
options.explanation: Randomized clinical trials demonstrate that combining IVIG and plasma exchange provides no added benefit over either treatment alone and substantially increases costs and catheter complications.

options.text: Admit to a general medical floor and discharge home on oral gabapentin if oxygen saturation remains >= 95%
options.explanation: Pulse oximetry remains completely normal until sudden fatal respiratory arrest occurs; ICU admission for serial FVC/NIF monitoring is mandatory in progressive GBS.

options.text: Administer oral ciprofloxacin 500 mg twice daily for 7 days to eradicate residual Campylobacter jejuni infection
options.explanation: Antimicrobial therapy weeks after diarrhea has resolved has no effect on the autoimmune molecular mimicry cascade of GBS and can worsen neuromuscular transmission.

subject: Medicine
topic: Idiopathic Intracranial Hypertension (IIH / Pseudotumor Cerebri)
stem:
A 27-year-old woman presents to the neurology clinic with a 2-month history of daily, throbbing generalized headaches that are worse upon waking in the morning and aggravated by bending forward or coughing. Over the past 3 weeks, she has noticed brief episodes of blackened vision lasting 5 to 10 seconds in both eyes when standing up (transient visual obscurations), as well as a rhythmic whooshing sound in her ears that corresponds to her heartbeat (pulsatile tinnitus). Her body mass index (BMI) is 36 kg/m2; she gained 12 kg (26 lbs) over the preceding 6 months. Physical examination reveals an alert woman with normal cranial nerve function except for bilateral visual fundus examination demonstrating marked bilateral papilledema with blurred optic disc margins and flame hemorrhages. Visual field automated testing reveals enlarged blind spots bilaterally without central visual acuity loss. Brain magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) with magnetic resonance venography (MRV) reveals an empty sella turcica, flattening of the posterior sclera, and bilateral transverse sinus stenosis without mass lesions, hydrocephalus, or dural venous sinus thrombosis. Lumbar puncture performed in the lateral decubitus position demonstrates an opening pressure of 340 mm H2O (normal <= 200 mm H2O in adults; > 250 mm H2O is diagnostic). Cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) analysis reveals normal cell count, glucose, and protein.

Which of the following represents the most appropriate initial pharmacological therapy for this patient?

options.text: Therapeutic serial lumbar punctures performed twice weekly to maintain opening pressure < 200 mm H2O
options.explanation: Serial lumbar punctures are painful, carry risks of CSF infection and epidural hematoma, and provide only transient CSF pressure relief (CSF regenerates at 20 mL/hour, replenishing within 6 to 12 hours).

options.text: Oral topiramate monotherapy at low dose (25 mg daily) without dietary modifications
options.explanation: While topiramate has weak carbonic anhydrase activity, acetazolamide is the proven first-line agent of choice with definitive clinical trial efficacy (IIHTT); weight loss is a mandatory cornerstone of disease remission.

options.text: Oral acetazolamide combined with a medically supervised weight-loss program
options.explanation: Idiopathic Intracranial Hypertension (IIH, formerly pseudotumor cerebri) predominantly affects young women of childbearing age with obesity or recent weight gain. DIAGNOSTIC CRITERIA (MODIFIED DANDY CRITERIA): (1) Symptoms and signs of elevated intracranial pressure (headache, pulsatile tinnitus, transient visual obscurations, papilledema); (2) Normal neurological examination except for cranial nerve VI (abducens) palsy; (3) Normal brain imaging excluding space-occupying lesions or hydrocephalus (neuroimaging signs include empty sella, flattening of posterior sclera, distention of perioptic subarachnoid space); (4) Elevated lumbar puncture opening pressure (> 250 mm H2O in lateral decubitus position); and (5) Normal CSF cytological and biochemical composition. FIRST-LINE MEDICAL MANAGEMENT: (a) ACETAZOLAMIDE: A carbonic anhydrase inhibitor that reduces cerebrospinal fluid secretion by the choroid plexus by up to 50%. The landmark NORDIC IIHTT (Idiopathic Intracranial Hypertension Treatment Trial) demonstrated that acetazolamide (titrated up to 1-4 g daily) significantly improves visual field function, reduces papilledema, and relieves headaches. (b) WEIGHT LOSS: Modest weight loss (5% to 10% of total body weight) has been demonstrated to normalize CSF opening pressure and achieve long-term clinical remission. (c) SURGICAL RESCUE: Optic nerve sheath fenestration or ventriculoperitoneal/lumboperitoneal shunting is reserved for patients with severe, rapidly progressive visual loss refractory to high-dose medical therapy.

options.text: Initiation of oral prednisone 60 mg daily for 4 weeks followed by a rapid steroid taper
options.explanation: Systemic corticosteroids are not recommended for routine IIH management due to severe rebound intracranial hypertension upon tapering, weight gain, and systemic metabolic toxicity.

options.text: Emergent placement of an optic nerve sheath fenestration before initiating any medical therapy
options.explanation: Surgical fenestration is an invasive intervention reserved for severe, rapidly deteriorating visual acuity or refractory papilledema failing maximum medical therapy, not initial management in mild visual field loss.

topic: Normal Pressure Hydrocephalus (NPH)
stem:
A 75-year-old man is brought to the outpatient clinic by his wife due to a 9-month history of progressive walking difficulty, urinary accidents, and memory lapses. His wife describes that he walks with a slow, shuffling manner and has had several near-falls. More recently, he developed urinary urgency that progressed to involuntary urinary incontinence, and he has trouble recalling recent appointments and names. On physical examination, the patient is alert and cooperative. Mini-Mental State Examination score is 23/30 with prominent executive dysfunction and psychomotor slowing. Cranial nerves are normal. Motor strength is 5/5 throughout with normal muscle tone. Deep tendon reflexes are symmetric and plantars are flexor. Sensation is intact. Gait assessment demonstrates a slow, wide-based, short-stepped gait with diminished step height; his feet appear glued to the floor ('magnetic gait') and he requires multiple small steps to complete a 180-degree turn. Brain MRI demonstrates ventriculomegaly with an Evans index of 0.38 (normal <= 0.30) that is markedly out of proportion to high-convexity cerebral sulcal enlargement, with flattening of sulci at the cerebral vertex and narrowing of the callosal angle.

Which of the following is the most appropriate next step to assess whether this patient will benefit from definitive cerebrospinal fluid shunting?

options.text: Proceed directly to surgical ventriculoperitoneal shunt placement without performing a diagnostic lumbar puncture tap test
options.explanation: VP shunting is an invasive neurosurgical procedure carrying significant risks of subdural hematoma, infection, and catheter malfunction; performing a prognostic tap test is standard to confirm shunt responsiveness.

options.text: Initiate oral donepezil 5 mg daily and memantine 10 mg twice daily for presumed Alzheimer dementia
options.explanation: Alzheimer disease presents primarily with early prominent episodic memory loss with cortical atrophy and preserved gait in early stages; NPH presents with early prominent gait apraxia and ventriculomegaly.

options.text: Initiate oral levodopa-carbidopa to treat presumed Parkinson disease gait freezing
options.explanation: Parkinson disease presents with resting tremor, cogwheel rigidity, and asymmetric bradykinesia; levodopa provides zero benefit for the apraxic gait of normal pressure hydrocephalus.

options.text: Perform a high-volume diagnostic lumbar puncture (removal of 30 to 50 mL of CSF) with quantitative timed gait assessment before and after the procedure
options.explanation: Normal Pressure Hydrocephalus (NPH) is a potentially reversible form of hydrocephalus characterized by the classic clinical triad ('wobbly, wet, wacky'): (1) GAIT DISTURBANCE: Typically the earliest and most prominent symptom, characterized as a magnetic, wide-based, apraxic gait with preserved motor strength; (2) URINARY INCONTINENCE: Urgency progressing to involuntary incontinence; and (3) COGNITIVE IMPAIRMENT: Subcortical dementia with psychomotor slowing, apathy, and executive dysfunction. NEUROIMAGING: Demonstrates ventriculomegaly (Evans index > 0.3) out of proportion to sulcal atrophy, with crowding of gyri at the cerebral vertex and bowing of the corpus callosum. DIAGNOSTIC ASSESSMENT (CSF TAP TEST): The single best predictor of clinical improvement from permanent surgical ventriculoperitoneal (VP) shunting is the HIGH-VOLUME LUMBAR PUNCTURE ('TAP TEST'). Approximately 30 to 50 mL of cerebrospinal fluid is removed. Objective, standardized gait assessment (e.g., 10-meter walk test, Timed Up and Go [TUG] test measuring time and steps required) is performed immediately before and 2 to 4 hours following the tap test. A demonstrable, quantitative improvement in gait velocity or reduction in step count confirms a positive tap test and carries a high positive predictive value (> 85-90%) for sustained clinical benefit from VP shunt placement.

options.text: Initiate oral acetazolamide 500 mg twice daily to reduce choroid plexus cerebrospinal fluid secretion
options.explanation: Acetazolamide has no demonstrated efficacy in normal pressure hydrocephalus and can induce volume depletion and electrolyte disturbances in elderly patients.

topic: Amyotrophic Lateral Sclerosis (ALS) Multidisciplinary Management
stem:
A 59-year-old man presents to the neurology clinic with a 7-month history of progressive weakness that began in his right hand with difficulty turning keys and buttoning shirts, followed by muscle twitching in both arms and difficulty walking. Over the past 2 months, he has noted slurred speech, choking episodes when drinking thin liquids, and orthopnea when lying flat in bed. Physical examination reveals emotional lability with inappropriate laughter (pseudobulbar affect), tongue atrophy with prominent fasciculations, and spastic dysarthria. Motor examination reveals asymmetric atrophy of the right first dorsal interosseous and thenar muscles with visible fasciculations, combined with hyperreflexia (3+ biceps and patellar reflexes bilaterally), a positive Hoffman sign on the right, and an extensor plantar response (positive Babinski) on the right. Sensory examination is completely normal. Electromyography (EMG) confirms active denervation (fibrillations and positive sharp waves) and chronic reinnervation changes in bulbar, cervical, and lumbosacral segments. Pulmonary function testing demonstrates an erect forced vital capacity (FVC) of 58% of predicted, which drops to 42% of predicted in the supine position.

Which of the following therapeutic interventions has the greatest proven efficacy in prolonging tracheostomy-free survival in this patient?

options.text: High-dose intravenous methylprednisolone 1,000 mg daily for 5 days followed by oral prednisone taper
options.explanation: ALS is a primary neurodegenerative disorder of motor neurons, not an inflammatory demyelinating disease; corticosteroids provide zero therapeutic benefit and accelerate muscle wasting.

options.text: Long-term intravenous immunoglobulin (IVIG) infusions administered every 3 weeks
options.explanation: IVIG is used to treat multifocal motor neuropathy (MMN, which presents with pure lower motor neuron weakness and conduction block on EMG), but is completely ineffective in ALS.

options.text: Emergent permanent tracheostomy and invasive mechanical ventilation before attempting non-invasive support
options.explanation: Invasive tracheostomy ventilation is reserved for patients who fail or decline non-invasive ventilation; non-invasive positive pressure ventilation is the non-invasive standard of care that prolongs survival.

options.text: Initiation of oral baclofen monotherapy without respiratory monitoring or ventilatory support
options.explanation: Baclofen is an adjunctive GABAB agonist that relieves muscle spasticity but has zero effect on disease progression, respiratory failure, or survival.

options.text: Initiation of non-invasive positive pressure ventilation (BiPAP) combined with oral riluzole therapy
options.explanation: Amyotrophic Lateral Sclerosis (ALS) is a fatal neurodegenerative disorder characterized by progressive loss of both Upper Motor Neurons (UMN: hyperreflexia, spasticity, Hoffman sign, Babinski sign) and Lower Motor Neurons (LMN: muscle atrophy, weakness, fasciculations) across multiple body regions (bulbar, cervical, thoracic, lumbosacral), with complete sensory sparing. (1) VENTILATORY SUPPORT (GREATEST SURVIVAL IMPACT): Diaphragmatic weakness manifests early as nocturnal hypoventilation, morning headaches, and orthopnea (demonstrated by a > 15-20% drop in FVC from erect to supine). Landmark randomized trials establish that timely initiation of NON-INVASIVE POSITIVE PRESSURE VENTILATION (NIV / BiPAP) is the single most powerful therapeutic intervention to prolong survival (extending life by 7 to 12 months) and maintain quality of life, far exceeding pharmacotherapy. Guidelines (AAN) recommend initiating NIV when: (a) FVC < 50% predicted, (b) Orthopnea or supine FVC drop > 15-20%, or (c) Nocturnal hypoxemia. (2) DISEASE-MODIFYING PHARMACOTHERAPY: RILUZOLE (50 mg orally twice daily) is a glutamate antagonist that inhibits voltage-gated sodium channels and presynaptic glutamate release, prolonging tracheostomy-free survival by approximately 2 to 3 months. (3) NUTRITION: Percutaneous endoscopic gastrostomy (PEG) is indicated for dysphagia and weight loss before FVC drops < 50% to minimize procedural respiratory complications.

stem:
A 29-year-old woman with relapsing-remitting multiple sclerosis (RRMS) diagnosed 2 years ago and managed with subcutaneous glatiramer acetate presents to the emergency department with a 3-day history of progressive right eye vision loss and eye pain worsened by ocular movements. She also reports a 2-day history of clumsy walking and tingling across both legs. She is afebrile with no signs of systemic infection or heat exposure (absence of Uhthoff phenomenon). Neurological examination reveals right eye visual acuity of 20/200, a right relative afferent pupillary defect (Marcus Gunn pupil), red-green color desaturation, and mild right optic disc swelling (anterior optic neuritis). Gait is moderately ataxic with a positive Romberg sign. Bilateral knee hyperreflexia and an extensor plantar response on the right are present. topic: Wernicke Encephalopathy and Thiamine Administration Timing
stem:
A 54-year-old man with a 20-year history of severe alcohol use disorder is brought to the emergency department by emergency medical services after being found disoriented, disheveled, and hypothermic in an alley. He has not consumed solid food for over a week according to peers. On physical examination, he is malnourished, disoriented to time, date, and place, and demonstrates impaired short-term recall and continuous fabrication of stories to fill memory gaps (confabulation). Cranial nerve examination reveals bilateral abducens (CN VI) nerve palsies with horizontal gaze-evoked nystagmus. Motor examination shows generalized muscle wasting with normal muscle tone. Cerebellar testing reveals prominent trunk and lower-extremity ataxia; he is unable to walk or perform tandem gait. Vital signs reveal blood pressure of 106/66 mm Hg, heart rate of 102/min, respiratory rate of 14/min, and core body temperature of 35.2 C (95.4 F). Point-of-care capillary blood glucose is 48 mg/dL.

Which of the following represents the most appropriate initial management sequence for this patient?

options.text: Administer a rapid bolus of 50% intravenous dextrose immediately and defer thiamine until full blood glucose normalization is achieved
options.explanation: Infusing dextrose alone in a severely thiamine-deficient patient accelerates intracellular thiamine depletion, triggering irreversible hemorrhagic necrosis of the mammillary bodies and Korsakoff syndrome.

options.text: Administer high-dose intravenous thiamine immediately prior to or concomitantly with intravenous dextrose
options.explanation: Wernicke Encephalopathy (WE) is an acute, life-threatening neurological emergency resulting from severe thiamine (vitamin B1) deficiency, predominantly occurring in chronic alcohol use disorder, severe malnutrition, hyperemesis gravidarum, or bariatric surgery. (1) CLASSIC CLINICAL TRIAD: (a) Encephalopathy (profound confusion, apathy, disorientation), (b) Oculomotor dysfunction (bilateral abducens nerve palsy, horizontal nystagmus, conjugate gaze palsy), and (c) Gait ataxia (wide-based cerebellar ataxia due to cerebellar vermis degeneration). Only approximately 15-30% of patients present with all three components simultaneously; high clinical suspicion is vital. (2) PATHOPHYSIOLOGY AND DEXTROSE DANGER: Thiamine pyrophosphate (TPP) is an indispensable cofactor for critical carbohydrate-metabolizing enzymes: pyruvate dehydrogenase, alpha-ketoglutarate dehydrogenase, and transketolase. In a severely thiamine-deficient state, administering an intravenous glucose or dextrose load increases glycolytic flux, causing rapid, catastrophic intracellular depletion of remaining thiamine stores. This triggers acute metabolic failure, focal lactic acidosis, and irreversible hemorrhagic necrosis of vulnerable brain structures (mammillary bodies, medial thalamus, periaqueductal gray). (3) MANAGEMENT RULE: High-dose intravenous thiamine (e.g., 500 mg IV every 8 hours) MUST ALWAYS BE ADMINISTERED PRIOR TO OR SIMULTANEOUSLY WITH INTRAVENOUS DEXTROSE. Delaying thiamine administration risks precipitating irreversible Korsakoff psychosis (anterograde/retrograde amnesia with confabulation) or fatal brainstem arrest.

options.text: Perform emergent brain MRI and lumbar puncture before administering any vitamins or glucose infusions
options.explanation: Wernicke encephalopathy is a clinical diagnosis; delaying thiamine and glucose administration for diagnostic neuroimaging or lumbar puncture can cause permanent irreversible brain damage.

options.text: Administer oral thiamine 100 mg daily with a normal hospital diet, as oral bioavailability is completely preserved in alcohol use disorder
options.explanation: Chronic alcoholism causes severe downregulation of intestinal thiamine transporters (THTR-1 and THTR-2); oral thiamine is poorly absorbed and completely inadequate for treating acute Wernicke encephalopathy.

options.text: Administer intravenous haloperidol 5 mg to treat confusion and confabulation before nutritional repletion
options.explanation: Antipsychotics do not treat the underlying metabolic defect, lower the seizure threshold, and worsen cerebellar ataxia and hypothermia.

topic: Epidural Hematoma and Emergent Surgical Indications
stem:
A 19-year-old college hockey player is struck on the right side of the head by a puck. He experiences a brief 30-second loss of consciousness, but rapidly awakens, answers questions appropriately, and insists he feels fine (lucid interval). Two hours later while sitting on the team bench, he develops a severe throbbing headache, becomes increasingly somnolent, and vomits repeatedly. Paramedics are summoned. On arrival in the emergency department, his Glasgow Coma Scale (GCS) score is 9 (E2V2M5). Physical examination demonstrates a dilated, sluggishly reactive right pupil (5 mm) and a briskly reactive left pupil (3 mm). Motor examination reveals left-sided hemiparesis with pronator drift and a positive left Babinski sign. Vital signs reveal blood pressure of 172/94 mm Hg, heart rate of 52/min, and respiratory rate of 12/min (Cushing triad). Emergent non-contrast head CT demonstrates a hyperdense, biconvex (lenticular) extra-axial collection along the right temporoparietal convexity that does not cross cranial suture lines. The hematoma volume is calculated at 42 cm3 with a 9-mm midline shift and compression of the right lateral ventricle.

Which of the following represents the most appropriate immediate definitive management for this patient?

options.text: Admit to the neurointensive care unit for continuous intracranial pressure monitoring and conservative serial head CT scans
options.explanation: Conservative observation is strictly limited to small (< 30 cm3), asymptomatic epidural hematomas with < 5 mm midline shift and normal GCS; observing a 42-cm3 hematoma with pupillary dilation and Cushing triad is fatal.

options.text: Administer intravenous mannitol 1 g/kg and hypertonic saline bolus as definitive standalone therapy without surgical intervention
options.explanation: Osmotic diuretics (mannitol/hypertonic saline) are temporary bridging maneuvers to transiently reduce brain edema en route to the operating room; they cannot arrest arterial bleeding or evacuate a 42-cm3 clot.

options.text: Emergent right-sided craniotomy and surgical evacuation of the hematoma with middle meningeal artery ligation
options.explanation: Epidural Hematoma (EDH) typically results from blunt trauma to the pterion (the thinnest portion of the lateral skull), causing a fracture of the temporal bone that lacerates the MIDDLE MENINGEAL ARTERY (a branch of the maxillary artery) or its associated dural veins. (1) CLINICAL COURSE: Classic presentation features a brief loss of consciousness, followed by a temporary symptom-free 'lucid interval', culminating in rapid, catastrophic deterioration as arterial blood strips the tightly adherent dura from the inner skull table. Progressive mass effect produces ipsilateral uncal herniation, compressing the ipsilateral oculomotor nerve (CN III parasympathetic fibers, causing an uncal blown pupil) and the ipsilateral cerebral peduncle (causing contralateral hemiparesis). Cushing triad (hypertension, bradycardia, irregular respiration) signals life-threatening brainstem compression. (2) NEUROIMAGING: Biconvex (lentiform), hyperdense extra-axial collection limited by cranial suture lines where the dura is firmly anchored. (3) SURGICAL CRITERIA (BRAIN TRAUMA FOUNDATION GUIDELINES): Immediate surgical evacuation via craniotomy is an absolute surgical emergency for: (a) Hematoma volume > 30 cm3 regardless of GCS score, OR (b) GCS score < 9 with midline shift >= 5 mm or pupillary asymmetry. Withholding emergent craniotomy for conservative observation or medical therapies in this rapidly expanding 42-cm3 arterial hematoma leads to fatal brainstem herniation.

options.text: Perform bedside burr hole trephination and leave an external ventricular drain in the right lateral ventricle
options.explanation: Burr hole trephination can easily miss a thick solid clotted epidural hematoma and fails to achieve hemostasis of the lacerated middle meningeal artery; formal craniotomy is required.

options.text: Administer intravenous tranexamic acid and high-dose dexamethasone to promote clot resorption
options.explanation: Corticosteroids are contraindicated in acute traumatic brain injury (CRASH trial proved increased mortality); medical therapies do not decompress mechanical arterial hematomas.

topic: Subdural Hematoma in Anticoagulated Elderly Patients
stem:
An 81-year-old man with non-valvular atrial fibrillation treated with warfarin (INR 2.8) is brought to the emergency department after his family noticed progressive confusion, somnolence, and unsteady gait over the past 5 days. Three weeks ago, he suffered a ground-level mechanical fall at home without reported loss of consciousness. On physical examination, the patient is obtunded, opening eyes only to loud voice and oriented only to person (GCS 12: E3V4M5). Neurological examination reveals mild right pronator drift, flattened right nasolabial fold, and hyperreflexia with an extensor plantar response on the right. Vital signs demonstrate blood pressure of 164/88 mm Hg and heart rate of 64/min. Emergent non-contrast head CT demonstrates a large, crescent-shaped, mixed-density (predominantly isodense-to-hypodense with dependent hyperdense areas) extra-axial fluid collection extending along the entire left cerebral convexity. The collection crosses cranial suture lines, measures 16 mm in maximal thickness, causes 10 mm of left-to-right midline shift, and compresses the left lateral ventricle.

Which of the following represents the most appropriate immediate sequence of interventions for this patient?

options.text: Proceed immediately to emergency craniotomy in the operating room while infusing fresh frozen plasma during the surgical procedure
options.explanation: Attempting neurosurgery without pre-reversing warfarin using 4F-PCC causes massive, uncontrollable intraoperative hemorrhage; 4F-PCC normalizes INR in minutes and must precede skin incision.

options.text: Administer oral vitamin K 10 mg and admit to the intensive care unit for serial neurological examinations over the next 48 hours
options.explanation: Oral vitamin K requires 24 hours to synthesize clotting factors and fails to provide rapid reversal; deferring surgery for a 16-mm hematoma with 10-mm midline shift causes fatal uncal herniation.

options.text: Administer intravenous recombinant factor VIIa (rFVIIa) monotherapy and observe without surgical decompression
options.explanation: Recombinant factor VIIa carries high arterial thromboembolic risk and is inferior to 4F-PCC for warfarin reversal; furthermore, 10 mm of midline shift requires mechanical surgical evacuation.

options.text: Immediate intravenous administration of 4-factor prothrombin complex concentrate (4F-PCC) and intravenous vitamin K, followed by urgent surgical evacuation (burr hole craniostomy or craniotomy)
options.explanation: Subdural Hematoma (SDH) in the elderly results from age-related cerebral cortical atrophy, which increases the distance between the brain surface and dural venous sinuses, placing mechanical traction on BRIDGING CORTICAL VEINS. Minor blunt trauma tears these fragile bridging veins, producing venous bleeding into the subdural space. (1) IMAGING: Crescentic (concave inward) collection that freely crosses cranial suture lines (dura is not anchored to sutures) but is limited by dural reflections (falx cerebri and tentorium cerebelli). Mixed density indicates chronic fluid with acute rebleeding ('acute-on-chronic' subdural hematoma). (2) MANAGEMENT SEQUENCE: (a) IMMEDIATE WARFARIN REVERSAL: Performing emergent neurosurgery with an elevated INR (2.8) leads to uncontrollable intraoperative hemorrhage. Immediate, rapid reversal with intravenous 4-factor Prothrombin Complex Concentrate (4F-PCC, 25-50 U/kg) normalizes the INR within 15 to 30 minutes, combined with intravenous vitamin K (10 mg) to sustain hepatic coagulation factor synthesis. Fresh frozen plasma is second-line and unacceptably slow. (b) URGENT SURGICAL EVACUATION: Brain Trauma Foundation guidelines mandate urgent surgical evacuation (burr hole craniostomy or craniotomy) for subdural hematomas with a thickness > 10 mm or midline shift > 5 mm, or whenever progressive neurological decline occurs.

options.text: Perform emergent lumbar puncture to reduce elevated intracranial pressure and drain subdural blood
options.explanation: Lumbar puncture in the presence of 10 mm of midline shift and asymmetric intracranial mass effect precipitates fatal transtentorial or tonsillar brain herniation.

subject: Medicine
topic: Uncal Herniation and the Kernohan Notch Phenomenon
stem:
A 45-year-old woman is admitted to the neurocritical care unit after sustaining a severe traumatic brain injury in a motor vehicle collision. Admission CT scan revealed an acute left-sided subdural hematoma with 8 mm of midline shift. Six hours after admission, her neurological status deteriorates acutely. Her GCS score drops from 11 to 6. On physical examination, her left pupil is 6 mm, fixed, and completely unreactive to light, while the right pupil is 3 mm and briskly reactive. Neurological examination reveals left-sided spastic hemiparesis with hyperactive left knee and ankle jerks and an extensor plantar response (positive Babinski sign) on the left side, with preserved motor movement on the right side. Vital signs show blood pressure of 184/96 mm Hg, heart rate of 48/min, and irregular respirations.

Which of the following anatomical mechanisms best explains the paradoxical presence of left-sided (ipsilateral) hemiparesis in the setting of an expanding left-sided intracranial mass lesion?

options.text: Subfalcine herniation causing mechanical compression of the contralateral right anterior cerebral artery
options.explanation: Subfalcine herniation forces the cingulate gyrus beneath the falx cerebri, compressing the anterior cerebral artery and producing contralateral lower-extremity motor weakness, not ipsilateral hemiparesis with an ipsilateral blown pupil.

options.text: Direct ischemic necrosis of the ipsilateral left internal capsule due to anterior choroidal artery compression
options.explanation: Infarction of the left internal capsule damages left descending corticospinal fibers before decussation, which produces contralateral (right-sided) hemiparesis, not ipsilateral hemiparesis.

options.text: Downward cerebellar tonsillar herniation through the foramen magnum compressing the lower medullary pyramids
options.explanation: Tonsillar herniation compresses the lower medulla and respiratory centers, causing sudden respiratory arrest and quadriparesis, not isolated ipsilateral hemiparesis with an isolated unilateral blown pupil.

options.text: Central transtentorial herniation causing bilateral diencephalic compression and decorticate posturing
options.explanation: Central herniation causes downward displacement of both cerebral hemispheres, presenting with initial small reactive pupils, Cheyne-Stokes breathing, and bilateral motor decorticate posturing.

options.text: Compression of the contralateral (right) cerebral peduncle against the rigid tentorial edge (Kernohan notch phenomenon)
options.explanation: Uncal (lateral transtentorial) herniation occurs when an expanding supratentorial mass (such as an acute left subdural hematoma) forces the medial temporal lobe (the uncus) downward and medially over the tentorium cerebelli into the posterior fossa. (1) CLASSIC PRESENTATION: (a) Compression of the ipsilateral (left) oculomotor nerve (CN III): The superficial, parasympathetic pupilloconstrictor fibers of CN III are compressed against the petroclinoid ligament, causing an ipsilateral dilated, 'blown', unreactive pupil. (b) Compression of the ipsilateral (left) cerebral peduncle (containing descending corticospinal motor tracts before their decussation in the caudal medulla): This classically produces CONTRALATERAL (right-sided) hemiparesis. (2) PARADOXICAL LOCALIZING SIGN (KERNOHAN NOTCH PHENOMENON): In severe or rapid herniation, the expanding left hemispheric mass pushes the entire midbrain across the tentorial incisura toward the opposite side. The CONTRALATERAL (right) cerebral peduncle is forced against the rigid, free edge of the CONTRALATERAL tentorium cerebelli (the Kernohan notch). Because the right corticospinal tract decussates in the medulla below, damage to the right cerebral peduncle results in IPSILATERAL (left-sided) hemiparesis—a classic 'false localizing sign'. Recognizing this phenomenon prevents catastrophic neurosurgical exploration of the incorrect cerebral hemisphere.

topic: Cauda Equina Syndrome vs Conus Medullaris Syndrome
stem:
A 44-year-old construction worker presents to the emergency department with severe, sharp lower back pain that radiates down the posterior aspect of both legs to his heels, which began after lifting heavy lumber 18 hours ago. Over the past 6 hours, he has felt a 'deadness' in his groin and inner thighs and noticed difficulty initiating urination; when he does void, he only passes small trickles of urine. Physical examination reveals an uncomfortable man in severe pain. Neurological examination reveals marked bilateral flaccid weakness of foot dorsiflexion (strength 2/5 bilaterally) and plantar flexion (strength 3/5 bilaterally). Sensation to light touch and pinprick is completely absent over the perianal, perineal, and medial upper thigh regions (S2-S5 dermatomes; saddle anesthesia). Patellar reflexes are 1+ bilaterally, and Achilles reflexes are absent (0/4) bilaterally. Digital rectal examination demonstrates absent anal sphincter tone and absent bulbocavernosus reflex. Post-void bladder ultrasound scan reveals a retained urine volume of 650 mL.

Which of the following represents the most appropriate immediate diagnostic and therapeutic strategy for this patient?

options.text: Perform emergent lumbosacral spine magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) followed by urgent surgical decompressive laminectomy within 24 to 48 hours
options.explanation: Cauda Equina Syndrome (CES) is a surgical emergency caused by mechanical compression of the lumbosacral nerve roots (L2 to S5) forming the cauda equina within the spinal canal below the termination of the conus medullaris (which ends at L1-L2). Most commonly caused by a massive central disc herniation (typically at L4-L5 or L5-S1). topic: Acute Angle-Closure Glaucoma
stem:
A 62-year-old woman of East Asian descent presents to the emergency department with severe, agonizing right eye pain and right-sided hemicranial headache that began 2 hours ago while watching a movie in a darkened cinema. She also reports blurred vision, seeing rainbow-colored halos surrounding streetlights, and persistent nausea with two episodes of emesis. On physical examination, she is in extreme distress, clutching her right orbit. Visual acuity in the right eye is 20/200 and in the left eye is 20/25. Examination of the right eye reveals intense conjunctival ciliary injection, a cloudy ('steamy') cornea, shallow anterior chamber depth, and a fixed, mid-dilated (5 mm) pupil that does not respond to light. The right globe feels rock-hard to gentle palpation through the closed eyelid. Applanation tonometry reveals an intraocular pressure (IOP) of 58 mm Hg in the right eye (normal 10 to 21 mm Hg) and 16 mm Hg in the left eye.

Which of the following represents the most appropriate immediate medical management sequence followed by definitive therapy for this patient?

options.text: Immediate administration of topical atropine 1% and cyclopentolate drops to relax the ciliary muscle and relieve pain
options.explanation: Topical atropine and anticholinergics cause pupillary dilation (mydriasis), which further bunches the peripheral iris into the filtration angle, completely occluding drainage and causing irreversible blindness.

options.text: Immediate administration of topical timolol, apraclonidine, and pilocarpine combined with intravenous acetazolamide (or mannitol), followed by emergent bilateral laser peripheral iridotomy
options.explanation: Acute Angle-Closure Glaucoma (AACG) is an ophthalmologic emergency occurring predominantly in predisposed individuals (hyperopia, shallow anterior chambers, East Asian or Inuit ancestry). Pupillary dilation (e.g., in a dark cinema or after sympathomimetic/anticholinergic drugs) causes the peripheral iris to contact the lens, blocking aqueous humor flow from the posterior chamber through the pupil (pupillary block). Pressure builds behind the iris, bowing it forward against the trabecular meshwork and abruptly occluding the iridocorneal filtration angle, causing intraocular pressure to surge (> 40 to 80 mm Hg). (1) CLINICAL PRESENTATION: Severe ocular pain, headache, halos around lights, nausea/vomiting, ciliary injection, cloudy/steamy cornea, and a fixed, mid-dilated pupil. (2) IMMEDIATE MULTI-AGENT MEDICAL THERAPY: Aimed at rapidly lowering IOP to protect the optic nerve: (a) TOPICAL TIMOLOL (beta-blocker) and APRACLONIDINE (alpha-2 agonist) to reduce aqueous humor synthesis; (b) TOPICAL PILOCARPINE (muscarinic cholinergic agonist) to induce miosis, pulling the peripheral iris away from the trabecular meshwork (administered once IOP drops < 40-50 mm Hg, as high IOP causes ischemic iris sphincter paralysis); (c) SYSTEMIC ACETAZOLAMIDE (intravenous carbonic anhydrase inhibitor) or IV MANNITOL (osmotic agent) for rapid vitreous dehydration. (3) DEFINITIVE SURGICAL THERAPY: Laser Peripheral Iridotomy (LPI) creates a full-thickness hole in the iris to equalize pressure between chambers. BILATERAL IRIDOTOMY IS MANDATORY because the contralateral eye has identical shallow anatomical angles and an 80% risk of acute closure.

options.text: Immediate performance of right eye anterior chamber paracentesis with an 18-gauge needle at the bedside without medications
options.explanation: Needle paracentesis through an acutely congested anterior chamber risks lens puncture, intraocular hemorrhage, and endophthalmitis; multi-agent pharmacotherapy followed by laser iridotomy is standard.

options.text: Administer intravenous methylprednisolone 1,000 mg daily for optic neuritis and consult neurology
options.explanation: Optic neuritis presents with central scotoma and painful eye movements without steamy cornea, mid-dilated fixed pupil, or intraocular pressure > 50 mm Hg; corticosteroids provide zero benefit in angle closure.

options.text: Unilateral right eye surgical trabeculectomy with no intervention or follow-up directed at the unaffected left eye
options.explanation: Laser peripheral iridotomy is the definitive procedure, not trabeculectomy; furthermore, failing to treat the contralateral eye leaves it at an 80% risk of subsequent acute angle closure.

subject: Medicine
topic: Central Retinal Artery Occlusion (CRAO)
stem:
A 68-year-old man presents to the emergency department 90 minutes after experiencing sudden, catastrophic, painless loss of vision in his left eye while eating breakfast. He describes that his vision went completely black within seconds, 'like a window shade was pulled all the way down,' and has not improved. He has a history of coronary artery disease, hypertension, hyperlipidemia, and a 40 pack-year smoking history. Physical examination reveals an alert man in no distress. Visual acuity in the left eye is limited to bare perception of hand motions; visual acuity in the right eye is 20/20. Pupillary examination reveals a marked left relative afferent pupillary defect (Marcus Gunn pupil). Slit-lamp biomicroscopy of the anterior segment is normal with normal intraocular pressure (14 mm Hg bilaterally). Dilated funduscopic examination of the left eye reveals diffuse retinal whitening and pallor with attenuation of retinal arterioles, segmentation of the blood column within retinal venules ('boxcarring'), and a prominent, circular 'cherry-red spot' visible in the central macula. Examination of the right eye fundus is normal.

Which of the following represents the most appropriate immediate management strategy for this patient?

options.text: Administer high-dose intravenous methylprednisolone 1,000 mg daily for presumed giant cell arteritis with ischemic optic neuropathy
options.explanation: Giant cell arteritis typically causes arteritic anterior ischemic optic neuropathy (AION) featuring a pale, swollen optic disc with headache, jaw claudication, and elevated ESR/CRP; CRAO presents with diffuse retinal pallor and a macular cherry-red spot.

options.text: Perform emergent vitrectomy with intravitreal injection of vascular endothelial growth factor (VEGF) inhibitors
options.explanation: Anti-VEGF therapy is indicated for central retinal vein occlusion (CRVO) with macular edema or diabetic retinopathy; it provides zero benefit for acute arterial occlusion.

options.text: Perform immediate bedside ocular massage, administer topical aqueous humor suppressants (e.g., timolol), and initiate an emergent acute ischemic stroke diagnostic evaluation
options.explanation: Central Retinal Artery Occlusion (CRAO) is the ocular analogue of an acute ischemic stroke, representing an end-organ vascular infarction most commonly caused by thromboembolism originating from an ipsilateral carotid artery atherosclerotic plaque (calcified or cholesterol emboli [Hollenhorst plaques]) or cardiogenic embolism (atrial fibrillation, valvular disease). (1) CLINICAL AND FUNDUSCOPIC FINDINGS: Sudden, profound, painless monocular visual loss with an afferent pupillary defect. Funduscopy demonstrates diffuse retinal clouding and pallor due to ischemic intracellular edema of the ganglion cell layer. The fovea centralis appears as a vivid 'CHERRY-RED SPOT' because the fovea is extremely thin and lacks ganglion cells, allowing the underlying richly vascular, red choroid (perfused by ciliary arteries) to show through. Retinal arteriole boxcarring reflects arrested blood flow. (2) IMMEDIATE OCULAR MANEUVERS: Retinal neural tissue tolerates ischemia for only 90 to 240 minutes before permanent necrosis occurs. Immediate maneuvers aim to dislodge the embolus into more distal peripheral branches and lower intraocular pressure: digital ocular massage (repeated cycles of firm pressure for 10-15 seconds followed by sudden release), topical IOP suppressants (timolol, apraclonidine), or anterior chamber paracentesis. (3) STROKE EQUIVALENT: CRAO carries a high immediate risk of concurrent or imminent cerebral stroke. Guidelines mandate immediate stroke evaluation, including brain MRI with diffusion-weighted imaging, carotid duplex ultrasound, echocardiography, and continuous cardiac telemetry.

options.text: Instill topical pilocarpine drops and perform emergent bilateral laser peripheral iridotomy
options.explanation: Pilocarpine and laser iridotomy treat acute angle-closure glaucoma (elevated IOP, painful eye, steamy cornea); IOP is normal (14 mm Hg) in CRAO.

options.text: Reassure the patient that retinal perfusion will spontaneously normalize within 24 hours and schedule outpatient follow-up
options.explanation: Retinal ischemia causes irreversible photoreceptor and ganglion cell death within 2 to 4 hours; CRAO is an emergency carrying catastrophic permanent blindness and high stroke risk.

topic: Giant Cell Arteritis with Visual Complications
stem:
A 74-year-old woman presents to the emergency department with a 3-week history of severe, throbbing right temporal headache, pain in her jaw muscles while chewing solid food that forces her to stop eating (jaw claudication), and aching stiffness in her shoulders and hips that is worst in the morning. This morning, she experienced two 5-minute episodes of blackened vision in her right eye (amaurosis fugax) that spontaneously resolved, but right eye vision remains blurred. Physical examination demonstrates an uncomfortable woman with marked tenderness, induration, and absent pulsations along the right superficial temporal artery. Visual acuity in the right eye is 20/80 and in the left eye is 20/20. Funduscopic examination of the right eye reveals a pale, swollen optic disc with blurred margins and scattered splinter hemorrhages (arteritic anterior ischemic optic neuropathy [A-AION]). Laboratory evaluation reveals:
- Erythrocyte sedimentation rate (ESR): 108 mm/hr (normal <= 30 mm/hr)
- Serum C-reactive protein (CRP): 42 mg/L (normal < 5 mg/L)
- Platelet count: 480,000/mm3

Which of the following represents the most appropriate immediate medical management for this patient?

options.text: Withhold all corticosteroids until a unilateral temporal artery biopsy is performed and histological confirmation of giant cells is verified
options.explanation: Delaying corticosteroids to obtain a temporal artery biopsy is a catastrophic error that results in permanent, irreversible bilateral blindness within 24 to 48 hours.

options.text: Initiate oral methotrexate 15 mg weekly as first-line monotherapy to avoid steroid-induced hyperglycemia and osteoporosis
options.explanation: Methotrexate has a slow onset of action (requiring 8 to 12 weeks) and is completely ineffective for acute inflammatory arterial ischemia; high-dose corticosteroids are mandatory.

options.text: Administer intravenous alteplase 0.9 mg/kg for presumed acute thrombotic occlusion of the posterior ciliary arteries
options.explanation: GCA is a chronic granulomatous autoimmune vasculitis, not a simple thromboembolic event; thrombolytics do not treat vasculitis and cause fatal systemic hemorrhages.

options.text: Immediate administration of high-dose intravenous pulse methylprednisolone (500 to 1,000 mg daily for 3 days) prior to obtaining a temporal artery biopsy
options.explanation: Giant Cell (Temporal) Arteritis (GCA) is a systemic granulomatous panarteritis of medium and large vessels, primarily affecting the extracranial branches of the carotid artery in patients > 50 years of age. (1) CLINICAL FEATURES: New-onset localized headache, scalp tenderness, jaw claudication (the highest positive likelihood ratio for GCA), polymyalgia rheumatica symptoms, marked ESR (> 50-100 mm/hr) and CRP elevation, and thrombocytosis. (2) VISUAL COMPLICATIONS: Occlusion of the posterior ciliary arteries leads to Arteritic Anterior Ischemic Optic Neuropathy (A-AION), manifesting as amaurosis fugax, sudden visual acuity loss, and a pale, edematous optic disc. Without immediate treatment, visual loss becomes IRREVERSIBLE, and involvement of the contralateral eye can occur within hours to days in up to 50% of untreated patients. (3) IMMEDIATE MANAGEMENT RULE: When visual symptoms or visual loss are present, IMMEDIATE HIGH-DOSE INTRAVENOUS PULSE METHYLPREDNISOLONE (500-1,000 mg/day for 3 days, followed by high-dose oral prednisone 1 mg/kg/day) MUST BE INITIATED IMMEDIATELY. (For patients without visual symptoms, oral prednisone 1 mg/kg/day is adequate). TREATMENT MUST NEVER BE DELAYED FOR TEMPORAL ARTERY BIOPSY. The histological features of granulomatous inflammation and giant cells persist on temporal artery biopsy for up to 2 to 4 weeks after initiating corticosteroid therapy.

options.text: Perform emergent right-sided superficial temporal artery endarterectomy
options.explanation: GCA involves segmental, diffuse transmural granulomatous destruction; surgical revascularization has no role and is technically impossible in small inflamed branches.

subject: Psychiatry
topic: Neuroleptic Malignant Syndrome (NMS) vs Serotonin Syndrome
stem:
A 28-year-old man with schizophrenia is brought to the emergency department by his family due to acute confusion, high fever, and extreme bodily stiffness over the past 24 hours. Four days ago, his outpatient psychiatrist increased his oral haloperidol dose from 5 mg to 15 mg daily and added intramuscular haloperidol decanoate for worsening persecutory delusions. On physical examination, the patient is obtunded, diaphoretic, and mute. Vital signs reveal blood pressure of 178/104 mm Hg, heart rate of 128/min, respiratory rate of 26/min, and core body temperature of 40.1 C (104.2 F). Physical examination reveals diffuse, severe 'lead-pipe' muscle rigidity throughout all four limbs, neck, and trunk. Deep tendon reflexes are 1+ bilaterally with down-going plantars; there is no ocular or extremity clonus. The skin is flushed and heavily soaked with perspiration. Laboratory evaluation reveals:
- Serum creatine kinase (CK): 48,000 U/L (markedly elevated; normal < 200 U/L)
- White blood cell count: 22,000/mm3 with 82% neutrophils
- Serum creatinine: 2.4 mg/dL (baseline 0.9 mg/dL)
- Serum potassium: 5.6 mEq/L

Which of the following represents the most appropriate immediate pharmacotherapeutic strategy for this patient?

options.text: Administer intravenous cyproheptadine 12 mg via nasogastric tube and maintain low-dose haloperidol to prevent acute psychotic relapse
options.explanation: Cyproheptadine is a 5-HT2A serotonin antagonist used specifically for serotonin syndrome; it has zero efficacy in NMS, and continuing haloperidol will result in fatal rhabdomyolytic cardiac arrest.

options.text: Administer high-dose intravenous acetaminophen 1,000 mg every 6 hours and apply standard ice packs without muscle-directed agents
options.explanation: Hyperthermia in NMS is generated peripherally by unremitting skeletal muscle contracture and central hypothalamic dopamine blockade, not hypothalamic prostaglandin synthesis; antipyretics like acetaminophen are ineffective.

options.text: Administer intravenous succinylcholine bolus to induce complete skeletal muscle relaxation
options.explanation: Succinylcholine triggers massive, lethal hyperkalemic cardiac arrest in patients with active rhabdomyolysis and denervation/muscle injury; it is strictly contraindicated.

options.text: Perform emergent hemodialysis to clear haloperidol decanoate from the plasma circulation
options.explanation: Haloperidol has a massive volume of distribution and high lipophilicity; hemodialysis does not remove haloperidol from tissues.

options.text: Immediately discontinue haloperidol, initiate aggressive external cooling and intravenous crystalloid hydration, and administer intravenous dantrolene and oral bromocriptine
options.explanation: Neuroleptic Malignant Syndrome (NMS) is a life-threatening idiosyncratic reaction triggered by potent dopamine D2 receptor antagonism (most commonly first-generation high-potency antipsychotics like haloperidol, fluphenazine, or abrupt withdrawal of dopamine agonists in Parkinson disease). (1) PATHOPHYSIOLOGY: Blockade of dopamine D2 receptors in the hypothalamus causes thermoregulatory set-point disruption (hyperthermia), and blockade in the striatum causes intense, unremitting muscle contracture ('lead-pipe' rigidity). (2) CLINICAL TETRAD: (a) Hyperthermia (temp > 38-40 C); (b) Extreme 'lead-pipe' muscle rigidity; (c) Autonomic instability (severe labile hypertension, tachycardia, tachypnea, profuse diaphoresis); and (d) Encephalopathy/altered mental status. (3) LABORATORY FINDINGS: Severe rhabdomyolysis with massive creatine kinase (CK) elevation (typically > 10,000 to 100,000 U/L), leukocytosis (15,000-30,000/mm3), and acute kidney injury from myoglobinuria. (4) DIFFERENTIATION FROM SEROTONIN SYNDROME: NMS is characterized by severe 'lead-pipe' rigidity and hyporeflexia, with slow onset over days. Serotonin syndrome is characterized by neuromuscular HYPERACTIVITY: hyperreflexia, spontaneous or inducible clonus, and tremor, with hyper-acute onset within hours of serotonergic exposure. (5) MANAGEMENT: Immediate cessation of antipsychotics, aggressive active cooling, and massive IV hydration. Specific pharmacotherapy: DANTROLENE (a skeletal muscle ryanodine receptor antagonist that inhibits calcium release from the sarcoplasmic reticulum, treating rigidity and hyperthermia) and BROMOCRIPTINE or AMANTADINE (dopamine receptor agonists that overcome hypothalamic/striatal dopamine blockade).

stem:
A 23-year-old woman with major depressive disorder managed with sertraline (100 mg daily) presents to the emergency department 6 hours after ingesting two doses of oral tramadol prescribed by an urgent care physician for an acute ankle sprain. She is accompanied by her roommate, who notes that the patient became progressively agitated, sweaty, and tremulous over the past 4 hours.
