topic: Hospital Delirium Prevention and Multicomponent Non-Pharmacologic Management
stem:
An 82-year-old man with mild cognitive impairment and benign prostatic hyperplasia is admitted to the medical ward on hospital day 3 for treatment of right lower lobe pneumonia with intravenous ceftriaxone and azithromycin. Over the past 12 hours, his mental status has fluctuated dramatically; he was lucid and conversant at breakfast, but became agitated, disoriented, and fearful at sunset, pulling out his peripheral intravenous catheter and urinary catheter, insisting that strange people are in his room trying to steal his clothes. On physical examination, he is restless, unable to sustain attention (cannot name the months of the year backward), and exhibits disorganized speech. Vital signs demonstrate blood pressure of 132/78 mm Hg, heart rate of 82/min, respiratory rate of 18/min, and oxygen saturation of 96% on room air. Focused evaluation reveals no hypoxemia, acute stroke, electrolyte derangement, or urinary retention. His bedside nurse requests an order for 'routine nighttime haloperidol or lorazepam' to ensure he stays asleep in bed.

Which of the following represents the most appropriate management approach for this patient's acute encephalopathy?

options.text: Administer intravenous lorazepam 1 to 2 mg every 4 hours as needed for agitation and insomnia
options.explanation: Benzodiazepines are a major independent precipitant of delirium, paradoxical disinhibition, respiratory depression, and fall injuries in elderly patients; they are contraindicated for delirium except in alcohol/sedative withdrawal.

options.text: Implement a multicomponent non-pharmacological delirium bundle (daylight exposure, nighttime dark/quiet environment, frequent reorientation, early mobilization, family presence, and removal of unnecessary tethers), withholding sedatives and antipsychotics unless the patient poses an immediate physical danger to self or others
options.explanation: Hospital Delirium is an acute, fluctuating disturbance in attention, awareness, and baseline cognition commonly precipitated by acute medical illness, hospitalization, infection, or medication exposure in vulnerable elderly patients. (1) PATHOPHYSIOLOGY AND RISK FACTORS: Underlying cognitive impairment, sensory deprivation, tethering (catheters, IV lines), sleep fragmentation, and anticholinergic drugs. (2) MANAGEMENT PARADIGM (AMERICAN GERIATRICS SOCIETY GUIDELINES): Randomized controlled trials (such as the Hospital Elder Life Program [HELP]) establish that MULTICOMPONENT NON-PHARMACOLOGICAL STRATEGIES are the gold-standard first-line intervention: (a) Environmental modifications: Day-night circadian synchronization (bright daytime lighting, opening window blinds, quiet/dark environment at night, minimizing vital sign checks between midnight and 6 AM); (b) Reorientation: Clocks, calendars, whiteboard with staff names, frequent verbal orientation, and familiar family presence; (c) Functional maintenance: Prompt removal of unnecessary physical restraints, bladder catheters, and IV lines; ensuring sensory aids (glasses, hearing aids) are in place; early progressive out-of-bed mobilization. (3) PHARMACOLOGICAL STEWARDSHIP: Multiple large randomized placebo-controlled trials have demonstrated that ANTIPSYCHOTICS (haloperidol, quetiapine) DO NOT SHORTEN DELIRIUM DURATION, REDUCE SEVERITY, OR IMPROVE MORTALITY, and they carry significant risks of extrapyramidal symptoms, QTc prolongation, and excess mortality in elderly patients with dementia (FDA black box warning). options.explanation: Physical restraints increase agitation, delirium severity, combativeness, strangulation risk, pressure ulcers, and aspiration without preventing falls.

topic: High-Risk Transient Ischemic Attack (TIA) and Dual Antiplatelet Therapy
stem:
A 67-year-old man presents to the emergency department 2 hours after experiencing an episode of sudden weakness and heaviness in his right hand and slurred speech while having lunch. The symptoms completely resolved spontaneously after 25 minutes, and he feels entirely back to his normal baseline on arrival. He has a history of essential hypertension treated with lisinopril and type 2 diabetes mellitus treated with metformin. On physical examination, he is alert and fully oriented. Neurological examination is completely normal, including cranial nerves, motor strength (5/5 throughout), sensation, cerebellar testing, and speech (NIHSS score is 0). Vital signs demonstrate blood pressure of 162/92 mm Hg, heart rate of 78/min, and oxygen saturation of 98% on room air. Emergent non-contrast head CT and brain MRI with diffusion-weighted imaging (DWI) show no acute intracranial hemorrhage or acute territorial cerebral infarction.

Based on his calculated ABCD2 risk score and landmark clinical trial evidence (POINT and CHANCE trials), which of the following represents the most appropriate initial antiplatelet strategy for secondary stroke prevention in this patient?

options.text: Initiate aspirin 81 mg monotherapy alone indefinitely, withholding clopidogrel to prevent gastrointestinal bleeding
options.explanation: Aspirin monotherapy is significantly inferior to DAPT in high-risk TIA (ABCD2 >= 4); omitting clopidogrel during the first 21 days leaves the patient at substantial risk for disabling recurrent ischemic stroke.

options.text: Initiate lifelong dual antiplatelet therapy with aspirin and clopidogrel continued indefinitely for secondary stroke prevention
options.explanation: Prolonging DAPT beyond 21 to 90 days provides no additional ischemic stroke reduction and dramatically increases the risk of fatal major extracranial and intracranial hemorrhage.

options.text: Initiate dual antiplatelet therapy (DAPT) with aspirin (loading dose followed by 81 mg daily) PLUS clopidogrel (300 to 600 mg loading dose followed by 75 mg daily) within 24 hours, continuing DAPT for 21 days followed by single antiplatelet monotherapy
options.explanation: Transient Ischemic Attack (TIA) carries a high risk of subsequent catastrophic ischemic stroke within the first 90 days, with the highest risk clustering within the first 48 to 72 hours. (1) ABCD2 RISK STRATIFICATION SCORE: (a) Age >= 60 years = 1 point; (b) Blood pressure >= 140/90 mm Hg at initial presentation = 1 point; (c) Clinical features: Unilateral weakness = 2 points, Speech disturbance without weakness = 1 point; (d) Duration: >= 60 minutes = 2 points, 10 to 59 minutes = 1 point, < 10 minutes = 0 points; (e) Diabetes mellitus = 1 point. In this patient: Age 67 (1 pt) + BP 162/92 (1 pt) + Unilateral right hand weakness (2 pts) + Duration 25 min (1 pt) + Diabetes (1 pt) = TOTAL ABCD2 SCORE OF 6 POINTS (HIGH RISK; score 6-7 carries an 8-12% stroke risk at 48 hours). (2) DUAL ANTIPLATELET THERAPY (POINT AND CHANCE TRIALS): Landmark randomized double-blind clinical trials (POINT and CHANCE) demonstrated that for HIGH-RISK TIA (ABCD2 score >= 4) or MINOR ISCHEMIC STROKE (NIHSS score <= 3), initiating DAPT (aspirin + clopidogrel) within 12 to 24 hours reduces the risk of recurrent ischemic stroke by approximately 25-30% compared to aspirin alone. options.explanation: Anticoagulation in non-cardioembolic TIA does not prevent recurrent stroke compared to antiplatelet agents and significantly increases fatal intracranial hemorrhage.

options.explanation: Thrombolysis is strictly contraindicated in TIA because neurological symptoms have fully resolved (NIHSS 0) and the risk of intracranial hemorrhage far outweighs any potential benefit.

topic: Bell Palsy (Idiopathic Facial Nerve Palsy)
stem:
A 32-year-old man presents to the urgent care clinic with sudden weakness of the right side of his face that he noticed upon waking this morning. When brushing his teeth, water drooled from the right corner of his mouth, and he felt his right eye burning and tearing. He denies limb weakness, sensory loss, visual changes, headache, or ear discharge. Physical examination reveals an alert man. Neurological examination demonstrates complete right-sided facial weakness: when asked to raise his eyebrows and wrinkle his forehead, there is complete absence of movement on the right side; when asked to close his eyes tightly, the right eyelid fails to close fully (lagophthalmos), and the right eyeball rolls upward and outward (Bell phenomenon); and when asked to smile, the right oral commissure does not elevate. Sensation over the face is symmetric and intact to pinprick. Extraocular movements, hearing, and all other cranial nerves are completely intact. Otoscopic examination of the external auditory canal and tympanic membrane reveals no vesicles, erythema, or discharge. Eye examination shows mild right conjunctival injection without corneal abrasion.

Which of the following represents the most appropriate pharmacological and supportive management for this patient?

options.text: Oral acyclovir 800 mg five times daily as standalone monotherapy without corticosteroids
options.explanation: High-level randomized trials prove that antiviral monotherapy provides zero therapeutic benefit compared to placebo in Bell palsy; corticosteroids are the definitive first-line therapy.

options.text: Perform emergent brain MRI with gadolinium and hospitalize for continuous stroke monitoring
options.explanation: Involvement of the forehead (upper face) definitively localizes the lesion to the peripheral facial nerve (LMN), completely ruling out an upper motor neuron stroke; neuroimaging is unnecessary in acute isolated Bell palsy.

options.text: Administer high-dose intravenous methylprednisolone 1,000 mg daily and perform emergent surgical facial canal decompression
options.explanation: Surgical facial nerve decompression carries substantial risks of permanent sensorineural hearing loss and is not recommended for acute Bell palsy; oral prednisone is standard of care.

options.text: Oral prednisone (60 to 80 mg daily for 7 to 10 days) initiated within 72 hours of symptom onset, combined with daytime lubricating artificial tears and nighttime eye ointment with eye taping
options.explanation: Bell Palsy is an acute, idiopathic, peripheral neuropathy of Cranial Nerve VII (facial nerve), likely triggered by herpes simplex virus reactivation causing edema and entrapment within the fallopian (facial) canal of the temporal bone. (1) UPPER VERSUS LOWER MOTOR NEURON WEAKNESS: (a) Central/UMN lesion (e.g., motor cortex stroke): Bilateral cortical motor innervation to the frontalis and orbicularis oculi muscles spares the upper face; therefore, forehead wrinkling is PRESERVED, and only the contralateral lower face is paralyzed. (b) Peripheral/LMN lesion (Bell palsy): All motor branches of CN VII are affected, resulting in ipsilateral paralysis of BOTH UPPER AND LOWER FACE (inability to wrinkle forehead, inability to close eye, flattened nasolabial fold, drooping mouth corner). (2) PHARMACOTHERAPY (AAN / AAO-HNS GUIDELINES): Multiple large randomized controlled trials (including the landmark Scottish Bell's Palsy Study) establish that ORAL CORTICOSTEROIDS (prednisone 60-80 mg daily for 7 to 10 days) significantly accelerate and increase the rate of complete facial nerve recovery (from ~70% to > 85-95%), provided they are INITIATED WITHIN 72 HOURS OF SYMPTOM ONSET. Antiviral monotherapy (acyclovir/valacyclovir) has NO benefit; combining antivirals with steroids offers minimal to no additional benefit over steroids alone. (3) CORNEAL PROTECTION: Incomplete eye closure (lagophthalmos) exposes the cornea to desiccation, keratitis, corneal ulceration, and permanent blindness. Eye protection with daytime lubricating artificial tears every 1-2 hours, nighttime lubricating ophthalmic ointment, and eye taping closed during sleep is MANDATORY.

options.text: Reassurance with observation alone, as over 95% of patients recover spontaneously without any medical intervention or corneal care
options.explanation: Untreated Bell palsy results in permanent facial asymmetry, synkinesis, or crocodile tears in 30% of patients, and failure to provide corneal lubrication causes corneal ulceration and permanent vision loss.

topic: Trigeminal Neuralgia (Tic Douloureux)
stem:
A 58-year-old woman presents to the clinic with a 6-week history of agonizing, lancinating right-sided facial pain. She describes the pain as sudden, sharp, electric shock-like jolts lasting between 5 and 30 seconds that shoot along her right lower jaw and right cheek. The episodes occur up to 20 times a day and are triggered by light sensory touch, such as brushing her teeth, applying makeup, washing her face, or encountering a cold breeze outdoors. She has stopped chewing food on the right side of her mouth to avoid triggering an attack. Neurological examination is completely normal: sensation to pinprick, light touch, and temperature across all three trigeminal nerve divisions (V1, V2, V3) is completely intact and symmetric bilaterally; corneal reflexes are normal; and motor function of the muscles of mastication (masseter and temporalis) is symmetric with normal jaw jerk. Brain MRI with dedicated high-resolution fiesta sequences demonstrates neurovascular compression of the right trigeminal nerve root entry zone by an aberrant loop of the superior cerebellar artery, with no demyelinating plaques, mass lesions, or brainstem infarcts.

Which of the following represents the most appropriate initial pharmacological therapy for this patient?

options.text: Oral ibuprofen 800 mg three times daily and acetaminophen 1,000 mg three times daily as first-line analgesic therapy
options.explanation: Standard non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs and acetaminophen have zero efficacy against neuropathic ephaptic firing in trigeminal neuralgia.

options.text: Scheduled oral oxycodone 10 mg every 4 hours for neuropathic pain control
options.explanation: Opioids are ineffective for the brief paroxysmal lancinating electric pain of trigeminal neuralgia and carry high risks of physical dependence, tolerance, and sedation.

options.text: Immediate referral for open posterior fossa craniotomy and microvascular decompression before attempting medical therapy
options.explanation: Microvascular decompression is an invasive intracranial neurosurgical procedure carrying risks of hearing loss, stroke, and CSF leak; conservative trial of first-line carbamazepine is mandatory before considering surgery.

options.text: Oral prednisone 60 mg daily for 4 weeks for presumed acute autoimmune trigeminal neuritis
options.explanation: Classical trigeminal neuralgia is a mechanical neurovascular compression disorder, not an inflammatory autoimmune neuropathy; corticosteroids are completely ineffective.

options.text: Oral carbamazepine (or oxcarbazepine), with baseline and follow-up monitoring of complete blood count and serum sodium concentrations
options.explanation: Trigeminal Neuralgia (TN, tic douloureux) is characterized by recurrent paroxysms of severe, sharp, lancinating, electric shock-like unilateral facial pain restricted to one or more divisions of the trigeminal nerve (most commonly V2 [maxillary] and V3 [mandibular], rarely V1 [ophthalmic]). (1) PATHOPHYSIOLOGY: Classical TN is caused by neurovascular compression of the trigeminal nerve root entry zone by an aberrant arterial loop (most commonly the superior cerebellar artery), leading to focal mechanical pulsatile demyelination, ephaptic cross-talk between sensory fibers, and hyper-excitable ectopic action potentials. (2) DIAGNOSTIC HALLMARKS: Paroxysms triggered by innocuous, light tactile stimuli (chewing, brushing teeth, light touch, wind); pain lasts seconds to < 2 minutes; neurological examination is characteristically completely normal (absence of sensory loss or motor weakness). (3) FIRST-LINE MEDICAL PHARMACOTHERAPY: CARBAMAZEPINE (titrated from 100-200 mg twice daily up to 1,200 mg daily) or OXCARBAZEPINE is the undisputed first-line treatment of choice, acting by blocking use-dependent voltage-gated sodium channels to stabilize hyper-excitable neuronal membranes and suppress high-frequency repetitive firing. (4) ADVERSE EFFECT MONITORING: Carbamazepine requires baseline and serial monitoring of Complete Blood Count (risk of aplastic anemia and agranulocytosis) and Serum Electrolytes (risk of Syndrome of Inappropriate Antidiuretic Hormone [SIADH] and severe hyponatremia). (5) SURGICAL RESCUE: Microvascular Decompression (MVD, Janetta procedure) is reserved for patients refractory to or intolerant of pharmacotherapy.

(1) PATHOPHYSIOLOGY: Classical TN is caused by neurovascular compression of the trigeminal nerve root entry zone by an aberrant arterial loop (most commonly the superior cerebellar artery), leading to focal mechanical pulsatile demyelination, ephaptic cross-talk between sensory fibers, and hyper-excitable ectopic action potentials. (2) DIAGNOSTIC HALLMARKS: Paroxysms triggered by innocuous, light tactile stimuli (chewing, brushing teeth, light touch, wind); pain lasts seconds to < 2 minutes; neurological examination is characteristically completely normal (absence of sensory loss or motor weakness). (3) FIRST-LINE MEDICAL PHARMACOTHERAPY: CARBAMAZEPINE (titrated from 100-200 mg twice daily up to 1,200 mg daily) or OXCARBAZEPINE is the undisputed first-line treatment of choice, acting by blocking use-dependent voltage-gated sodium channels to stabilize hyper-excitable neuronal membranes and suppress high-frequency repetitive firing. (4) ADVERSE EFFECT MONITORING: Carbamazepine requires baseline and serial monitoring of Complete Blood Count (risk of aplastic anemia and agranulocytosis) and Serum Electrolytes (risk of Syndrome of Inappropriate Antidiuretic Hormone [SIADH] and severe hyponatremia). (5) SURGICAL RESCUE: Microvascular Decompression (MVD, Janetta procedure) is reserved for patients refractory to or intolerant of pharmacotherapy. Lancinating facial pain triggered by light touch with normal neuro exam is Trigeminal Neuralgia; first-line therapy is carbamazepine with CBC and sodium monitoring.
